uncited: It sets itself apart from standard DOM by using these 2D propagation maps instead of a full 3D directional grid for the transport step, and from [Isotropic Residuum Propagation](4122-isotropic-residuum-propagation.md) by handling the full anisotropic propagation before potentially switching to isotropic residuum methods.
*   **Input:** A 3D voxel grid representing the medium with absorption coefficient $K_a$, scattering coefficient $K_s$, and phase function $p(\omega, \omega')$.
Boundary conditions (incoming radiance) and self-emission radiance.
**3D Grid:** Stores medium properties ($K_a, K_s$) and radiance buffers.
**Light Propagation Maps (LPMs):** A set of 2D arrays.
Each LPM corresponds to a face of the coarse 3D grid.
*   Each element $(r,s)$ in an LPM stores a set of rays originating at $(r,s)$ with directions sampled from the unit sphere $S^2$.
*   High spatial resolution compared to the storage grid.
*   Create LPMs for each face of the 3D grid.
*   If $p == 0$: Initialize $L_{r,s}^{i,0}$ with boundary conditions (incoming radiance).
*   Update ray radiance $L_{r,s}^{i,t}$ using Eq. (3) and $U_{d,pprev,xyz}$.
*   **Memory Complexity:** Proportional to the size of the 3D grid (for $I$ and $U$ buffers) plus the size of all LPMs.
